1. Introduction

Despite the increase in interest and consumption, electric and hybrid vehicles (EV and HEV, respectively) are far from being a market novelty. In the past, those cars strongly competed with combustion cars. In a timeline, Figure S1 illustrates the history of EV and HEV and their battery types developed over the years (Høyer, 2008; Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019; Xie and Lu, 2020).

The history of EV begins in the mid-19th century, closely related to the history of batteries. In 1859, the Belgian Gaston Planté presented the first lead-acid battery, becoming important for these vehicles and, later, for automobiles with an internal combustion engine (ICE), created by Karl Benz in 1879, allowing the commercial production of vehicles with ICE (Høyer, 2008).

As early as 1901, Thomas Edison created nickel-iron batteries for EV. The storage capacity was 40% greater than lead batteries, but with higher production costs. In the early 19th century, three propulsion technologies were competing in the automobile market: the electric, steam, and gasoline cars (Angeline and Rajkumar, 2020; Høyer, 2008).

The 1880s, 1900s were the most intense decades for the development of EV. In 1903, about 53% of vehicles registered in New York City ran on steam, 27% on gasoline, and 20% were electric. In the 1910s, the trajectory of EV reached a peak in the USA with 3,000 electric cars. Then, the EV market declined. Several reasons contributed to its decline: the oil discoveries in Texas, allowing the price of gasoline to decrease; the replacement of the crank trigger ignition by the electric starter; the increase in the number of highways in the United States which require greater vehicle autonomy; and the system created by Henry Ford for mass production of automobiles, leading to a reduction in the price of gasoline cars, reaching half the price compared to electric ones. In post-war Japan, the EVs became quite popular because of fuel rationing, but their production was discontinued in the 1950s when rationing ceased (Høyer, 2008).

In the 1960s, electric automobiles attracted large automakers' attention, since environmental problems were given greater attention. Debates about energy generation and consumption were taken into consideration due to climate change: fossil fuel for transportation makes ICE vehicles responsible for 27% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. Even with several initiatives to bring them back to the market in the period, neither pure electric cars nor hybrids could compete with conventional cars due to the aforementioned issues (Angeline and Rajkumar, 2020; Høyer, 2008).

In the late 1980s, the concerns about pollution in large urban centers focused attention on the EV towards sustainable development, the need to use an alternative energy source, and new technologies (Larcher and Tarascon, 2015). According to Browne et al. (2012), the barriers to alternative fuels, vehicles and policies to raise innovative technologies towards sustainable development depend on geographical boundaries, which are strictly related to consumer choices, jurisdictions, and the stage of technological innovation (Browne et al., 2012).

New policies to face the environmental issues were observed beginning in the 1960s with the EPA creation (in the USA) and the UN Conference in Stockholm, which resulted the Brundtland report in the 80s (United Nations, 1983), as well as the UN Sustainable Development Goals (United Nations, 2020). The enforcement of new policies move the market towards clean technologies.

In the 1990s, the HEV was introduced through public-private partnerships of different companies. In 1999, Honda was the first company to launch a hybrid in the American market and was an immediate success. In the 2000s, several vehicles were released to the market by different companies. The return of HEV and EV in the USA is mainly focused on the country's energy security, as it would allow oil, largely imported from politically unstable places, to be replaced by electricity, produced entirely in the country itself (Høyer, 2008; Miao et al., 2019).

For developing countries, such as members of BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa), the EV can become an important alternative to sustainable development. If policies encouraging their use are adopted according to the development of the fleet, it would make the use of the electric car bring effective strategic and environmental benefits in the long term (Cheng et al., 2017; Høyer, 2008; Pistoia and Liaw, 2018). In cases in which electricity is generated from fossil fuels (e.g., coal and natural gas), the emissions are concentrated on the energy-generating sources, not on large centers, as currently occurs (Ajanovic and Haas, 2019; Høyer, 2008).

Although LIBs are widely used in portable devices, electric cars, industrial and domestic equipment, these batteries still have materials that can cause environmental issues and safety problems (Tedjar and Foudraz, 2006; W. Zhang et al., 2018a): Li, Mn, Co, and Ni in the cathode; Fe in the casing; Al and Cu in the anode current collector; graphite, Nb, Li and Ti in the anode; and organic compounds, such as electrolytes. Although some of these elements are essential micronutrients for some plants growth, in excess in the environment, these metals can cause an adverse effect, being toxic, persistent, and bioaccumulative, impairing the organism survival, growth, and reproduction (Ali et al., 2019). Most battery electrolytes are organic solvents, volatile compounds, flammable, and toxic to humans and the environment (Wuschke et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2018).

Likewise, some LIB raw materials are considered critical in some countries/regions, making the recycling important from economic and environmental perspectives. Social issues are meaningful for reaching sustainable development. Cobalt, for instance, is often extracted in regions where safe working conditions are not always guaranteed. The Democratic Republic of the Congo accounts for about 60% of the global market share; 20% comes from its artisanal mining sector (Statista, 2019). For these reasons, the recycling of batteries in the end-of-life may lessen the negative impacts of the EV and HEV use (Aichberger and Jungmeier, 2020).

Despite that, an evaluation of ICE and EV/HEV's global market is needed for future decision-making, mainly in the USA and Europe, where the market is likely to rise in the next years, and in the BRICS, since these countries represent local leadership and global economic importance. For approaching this issue, the present study is divided as follows: I) Statistic evaluation of the global market, growth rate and EV production; II) Characteristics of EV and HEV batteries; III) Current and future recycling routes; and IV) Future perspectives.

2. Objectives and methodology

The main objective of this review was to analyze the influence of EV batteries on society and the environment, establishing crucial factors that affect the future generation of such waste globally, allied to the current and future recycling routes technology in order to achieve sustainable development. The secondary objectives and adopted approaches are listed as follows:

●

Data about conventional and electric/hybrid vehicles. Statistics published by Statista, World Bank Group, and others to gather data related to production and market around the world to establish the correlation between different indices;

●

Calculating and analyzing the future trend of the EV/HEV market.

●

Recycling routes and their challenges. Data collection for consolidated processes and new development, presenting technical aspects and environmental issues aiming at the SDGs n° 7, 9, 11, 12, and 13;

●

Importance of recycling due to the criticality of the metals;

●

Achieving the circular economy of electric vehicles throughout the recycling;

Along with these objectives, the current practices to deal with vehicle batteries used nowadays and recycling methods adopted are also presented in this paper, in addition to the benefits and issues associated with electric vehicle use and future perspectives. The present study is limited by the current data of ICE and EV/HEV market worldwide, patents available for battery recycling and new trends published in the scientific journal (in English).

3. Statistics

3.1. Global market of vehicles and growth rate

Fig. 1a shows the number of vehicles in use worldwide increased from 0.89 billion to 1.28 billion of units from 2005 to 2015, most of which are in Europe – 30.2% of the global vehicle units (Fig. 1b). The growth rate has remained constant in the USA and Europe, whereas the number of vehicle units in the world has increased, following the Chinese rate. The number of vehicles on the streets in China rose by 415% between 2005 and 2015, whereas in Europe, in the USA and globally the growth stood at 20%, 11%, and 44%, respectively. According to present data, around 1.83–1.97 billion vehicle units are expected globally in 2030, out of which 20–22% in China (OICA, 2018; Wagner, 2020a).

The distribution of vehicles worldwide is related to the highest gross domestic product (GDP) and population. Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 show the data correlation among BRICS countries, Europe and the USA. Fig. 2 shows a linear relationship between the number of vehicles and the GDP in South Africa, Russia, Brazil, and India, while Fig. 3 depicts no significant correlation or trend between vehicles per inhabitant and GDP.

The two outliers in all observations are the USA and Europe due to their higher GDP than BRICS countries, in addition to having an elevated number of vehicles in use even per inhabitant. Europe, the USA, and China, regions with the highest number of vehicles, stand out in regard to GDP (15592.8, 21427.7, and 14342.9 billion dollars, respectively), indicating that there is a correlation between GDP and vehicles in use (OICA, 2018; The World Bank, 2020a; 2020b).

Fig. 4 correlates the number of vehicles in use with the population, making South Africa, Russia, and Brazil closely related. In this case, the outliners are China and India due to the number of inhabitants in each country (1.39 and 1.37 billion people, respectively) (OICA, 2018; The World Bank, 2020a; 2020b). As in the e-waste generation, the GDP difference in both countries increases the total e-waste generation (Kumar et al., 2017). The same effect was observed in regard to vehicles.

3.2. Production of electric vehicle

Fig. 5 shows the number of new EV sales and in use from 2005 to 2019. Indeed, compared with the total number of vehicles, the share of EV is still low, but the data has demonstrated that it is in exponential growth. It can be observed that EV shows the same behavior as ICE, i.e., countries with the highest GDP have the highest market share of EV. In 2017, Norway accounted for for 39.2% of the EV market, followed by Iceland (11.7%), Sweden (6.3%), Netherlands (2.7%), Finland (2.6%), and China (2.2%), whereas the UK, France, Germany, the USA, New Zealand, Canada, and Japan stood at less than 2% each (IEA, 2018).

The increase of EV production is part of the fulfillment of the Paris climate agreement goals and sustainable development goals by the United Nations, such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions, affordable and clean energy, economic growth, sustainable cities, responsible consumption and production, and climate action (Gigliotti et al., 2019; Pavez et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020).

The growth in the number of vehicles in circulation in China, the USA, and Europe is depicted in Fig. 6. The Chinese share increased from 8% in 2014 to 39% in 2018 (a 3711% growth), while the number of electric cars in circulation in the USA and Europe increased by 344% and 742%, respectively (IEA, 2018). In 2019, the global market of EV amounted to 115 billion dollars, and it is estimated to be about 567.2 billion dollars worldwide in the near future (Wagner, 2020c).

The use of EV and HEV shall decrease the amount of CO2 released in the cities. On the other hand, the electricity source turns out to be a concern as the increased use of electricity from renewable sources softens EV carbon footprint, and the evaluation of pollution is strictly related to coal as the primary energy source (Abdallah and El-Shennawy, 2013). In the USA, the EV energy charging demand shall push up electricity use by 35% until 2030 reaching 5.193 billion kWh, and the share of coal power generation stands at 13.5%. The Chinese share of coal power amounts to 44.8%, whereas the EV share stands at 39.5% worldwide(Statista, 2019).

As the demand for EV and HEV shall increase in the next years, batteries consumption will probably follow the same trend. Electricity and heat generation account for 41.5% of CO2 released per capita worldwide, whereas transportation accounts for 24.3%. Around 40% of energy generation comes from coal source (Statista, 2019), which means that pollution in countries with high non-renewable energy will be transferred from urban centers to regions where coal energy is generated (Bobeth and Kastner, 2020). The choice to exchange ICE vehicles for EV and HEV should accompany the change in the energy matrix. Generation's The expectation to reach 50% of electricity generation relying on wind and solar energy in 2040 may support the decline in CO2 release (IEA, 2020b). Also, different batteries and composition configurations are designed aiming at the same achievement.

4. Electric vehicles batteries

Although EVs are less vulnerable than fossil fuel prices, they are susceptible to a volatile commodity market (Adhikari et al., 2020). Since the LIB production is likely to increase in order to meet the EV market needs, the cobalt supply will follow the demand. Its mining is dependent on nickel and copper production since cobalt is extracted from these resources and has no ore of its own.

Supply-demand imbalances and geopolitical constraints shall persist in The Democratic Republic of Congo, owing to social issues in this politically unstable region and market control associated with exportation restriction. It will impact the global cobalt price, and consequently the final EV and HEV price. Despite the price increase due to the demand, another consequence would be obtaining unexplored resources as an economic reality, such as mining wastes and recycling (Alves Dias et al., 2018).

In general, a battery pack is composed of US$1,764 of cobalt, US$1,433 of nickel, US$1,005 of lithium carbonate, and US$536 of graphite (Duarte Castro et al., 2021; Statista, 2019). It changes as the composition of the batteries varies. There are different configurations of batteries in the market for several purposes.

4.1. Lithium-ion batteries

The development of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) at the end of the 20th century led to a great advance in the energy storage sector and technological advances in the portable electronics and electric cars sectors (Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Compared with other batteries, their properties include high energy density, memory effect almost null, and low self-discharge rate, producing more autonomous, durable, and lightweight equipment (Hannan et al., 2018).

Figure S2 depicts the structure of the most common LIBs currently used in HEV and EV. The most challenging aspect of battery recycling is its many different types, sizes, compositions, changing weight, cost, and efficiency (Elwert et al., 2016). Such batteries are organized into three groups: cells (batteries alone), modules (a group of cells), and packs (a group of modules). Cylindrical batteries comprise 444 cells per module and 16 modules per pack, totalizing 7104 cells in one pack. The prismatic one has 96 cells per pack, whereas pouch batteries have 192 cells per pack(Harper et al., 2019).

Li-ion is the generic name for the active materials in these batteries, and there are different types in the market (Lv et al., 2018; Passerini and Scrosati, 2016), and their constituent components are two electrodes, the anode, the cathode, a separator, and an electrolyte for its performance as a power generator (Figure S3) with working voltage more than 3V(W. Zhang et al., 2018b). Moreover, LIBs have a metallic casing (e.g., steel) or a plastic casing, and an electronic control unit (Zeng et al., 2014). Lithium ions flow from anode to cathode through connected terminals when the battery is in use, and the electrons leave the negative electrode towards the positive electrode thus generating electric current (Zhang and Ramadass, 2012). In the charging cycle, the process is the opposite (Miao et al., 2019). These batteries are also known as “rocking chair battery”.

The separator is responsible for not allowing the direct contact of the positive and negative electrode, avoiding a short circuit; it is also a safety device when it comes to overheating (Santhanagopalan and Zhang, 2012). However, the separator is made of microporous material of polyethylene (PE) or polypropylene (PP), which allows the maximum passage of Li-ions (Zeng et al., 2014).

The electrolyte is composed of lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent; the most common ones include LiPF6, LiBF4, LiClO4, and LiSO2 dissolved in organic solvents propylene carbonate, ethylene carbonate, or dimethyl sulfoxide (Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2014). However, organic solvents are flammable and can contaminate the environment if released. For this reason, solid polymeric electrolytes have been developed such as poly (ethylene oxide) - PEO, poly (propylene oxide) - PPO, poly (acrylonitrile)) - PAN, and poly (methyl methacrylate) – PMMA (Zeng et al., 2014).

The anode is the material responsible for conducting the electrons and allowing Li-ions to flow in its structure (Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019). It is composed of a copper current collector (Cu foil), an organic binder (PVDF), and an active material (graphite) (W. Zhang et al., 2018b). The cathode consists of an aluminum current collector, a PVDF organic binder, and an active material – a phosphate or oxide of a lithiated transition metal, which must also allow the Li-ions to flow freely(Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019). Unlike (the) anode, (the) cathode active material is very diverse, as it depends on the desired cost and properties (Kabir and Demirocak, 2017; Miao et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2014), but different types of anodes have been explored to improve efficiency and safety. A few examples of cathode and anode used in LIBs are presented as follows:

4.1.1. Cobalt lithium oxide (LiCoO2) – LCO

The LCO cathode type is most used in portable electronics and has also been reported in EV like the Tesla Roadster and Smart Fortwo. The cathode released in 1991 has a high energy density and low self-discharge, but a short lifetime, in addition to being expensive due to the high cobalt content. Also, the thermal stability is considered low since the layered structure of the LCO and the graphite anode is limited to 1C current(Hannan et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2019; Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.2. Lithium manganese oxide (LiMn2O4) - LMO

Lithium and manganese oxide (LiMn2O4) cathode, or LMO, has a spinel structure that improves the Li-ions to flow allied to thermal stability. Moreover, magnesium is cheaper than cobalt (Kabir and Demirocak, 2017; Miao et al., 2019). On the other hand, there are two main problems: a) the low internal resistance of the cells allows faster charging and discharging limited to a current lower than 120mAh/g, and b) shorter lifetime. Nevertheless, LMO cathode is used in various vehicles, such as the Nissan Leaf, Chevy Volt, and BMW i3(Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.3. Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) – LFP

Lithium iron phosphate cathode (LFP) is an active material that offers excellent safety and thermal stability properties but has some performance problems(Forte et al., 2020; Hannan et al., 2018). It is produced with nano-scale phosphate materials and offers significant safety and thermal stability, has low resistance to ion flow, tolerates high temperatures, overcharging, and an excellent power efficiency producing 160mAh/g current. However, it has a high self-discharge that can be improved with electronic control. It increases the product price. Although moisture reduces its lifetime, the LFP cathode is becoming popular among motorhomes (Hannan et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.4. Lithium nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (LiNiCoAlO2) – NCA

The NCA cathode type is used for special applications offering high specific energy, good specific power, and long service life compared to other types of LIBs. On the other hand, the disadvantages are related to safety and manufacturing costs. High energy and power densities and good service life make NCA cathode an interesting option for EV and HEV. Tesla company uses it in some cases(Hannan et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.5. Lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (LiNiMnCoO2) – NMC

One of the most successful Li-ion systems is nickel, manganese, cobalt (NMC) oxide cathodes, 33% nickel, 33% manganese, and 34% cobalt (Wang et al., 2020), in which the high specific energy from nickel is combined with the manganese spinel structure. The mixture of good properties has been attracting the attention of EV manufacturers, such as BMW, Chevy, and Nissan, who already use them in their cars (Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.6. Lithium Titanate (Li4Ti5O12) - LTO

LTO anodes have been known since the 1980s, being used in LMO or NMC batteries. It has a spinel structure that does not undergo structural change during lithiation. Besides, the material increases the lifetime of LIBs with high security (Hua et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2019; Xu, 2014). However, it presents performance problems in the diffusion of lithium ions and in electronic conductivity, which can be solved with nanostructures and dopants, respectively (Hannan et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2019). LTO anodes dopped with graphene have drawn attention regarding the improvement of electronic conductivity (Cai et al., 2017).

LTO anodes are known for not undergoing lithium coating during rapid loading and long-term cycling, which leads to long service life and safety; on the other hand, they have as a disadvantage, a low energy density that may be suitable for automotive applications (Takami et al., 2018a). Notwithstanding, LTO anode-type is used by Japanese manufacturers such as Mitsubishi's i-MiEV and Honda Fit EV (Hannan et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2019).

4.1.7. Titanium niobium oxide (TiNb2O7) - TNO

In addition to the LTO, TNO anodes are being explored more recently. During lithium storage, the electrochemical properties were studied to develop an alternative anode with high capacity, fast charging, and longer service life than LTO. Cycle life tests indicate that the TNO/NMC batteries have up to 14000 cycles at 80% capacity retention, which is considered competitive compared to LTO/NMC system. The test is important mainly to decide specific applications of batteries according to the performance requirements (Kellner et al., 2018; Takami et al., 2018b).

High-density TNO anode (HD-TNO) composed of carbon-coated particles with secondary spherical micro-size of TNO exhibited high rate capability, long service life, and high volumetric capacity. TNO/NCM batteries have shown high energy density, fast charging, and a long life cycle for automotive applications, such as electric cars with long driving ranges for fast charging (Babu and Shaijumon, 2020; Duesenfeld, 2020; Griffith et al., 2019; Takami et al., 2018a).

4.2. Batteries of the future for electric vehicles

As LIBs are known as explosive, flammable components have been replaced without losing efficiency (Motavalli, 2015). The speed of charging and discharging of batteries is also a requirement, since ICE vehicles can be quickly refueled at gas stations; therefore, the slow discharge gives – at least - an autonomy similar to that which ICE vehicles allow (Horn et al., 2019; Rajashekara, 2013). One of the most decisive points is the price: EV and HEV must be accessible, regarding car structure, such as electronic devices and battery composition, the latter being crucial, as cobalt is considered a critical material (European Commission, 2017, 2019, 2017; Rajashekara, 2013). Despite all the development that LIBs have already undergone, several requirements must be improved for greater use of HEV and EV by the population.

The cathode is the main material in batteries, as it is the main responsible for determining the working voltage, energy density, and rate capability (Liu et al., 2016). A cathode that has attracted attention is Li2MSiO4 (M = Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni) since there are Li-ions in its structure, which can generate a high theoretical specific capacity (~330Ah/kg); however, its cyclic performance is still far from ideal(Xu et al., 2013).

The lithium nickel oxide cathode (LNO) is considered promising due to its high specific energy and low cost; nevertheless, it still forms a self-passivation layer during its use (Miao et al., 2019). The LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 (LNMO) cathode has also been considered a promising material, as it can reach a voltage of 4.5V if combined with graphite, and a high theoretical energy density (630 Wh/kg) (Shariatinia, 2021). However, this cathode requires a stable electrolyte at 5V, which does not exist at an affordable cost (Passerini and Scrosati, 2016).

According to Xu et al. (2013), the most promising cathodes are Li–O2, Li–S/C, and Li2S–Si, due to their high energy density, but many structural problems still need to be solved for its use as a battery cathode (Xu et al., 2013).

Graphene has been used in the cathode material to improve the LIB performance since it has good chemical stability, high electron mobility and high thermal conductivity (AL-Saedi et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2017; Chen and Tian, 2020).

Park et al. (2021) studied the use of graphene coating on NCA cathode to improve the electrode capacity, which demonstrated better performance than conventional batteries with high energy storage (Park et al., 2021).

In the case of anodes made from graphite, the charge/discharge process causes Li plating and dendrite growth resulting in a severe safety issue. The use of graphene layers in the graphite diminishes it and improves the high capacity value, high rate performance and low coulombic efficiency. Nevertheless, the graphene as anode material has drawn interest due to its high conductivity, mechanical strength, high charge carrier mobility and high surface area (Cai et al., 2017).

As for anodes, many materials are being considered as promising. Metal lithium has the lowest electrochemical potential and a very high specific capacity (3860Ah/kg) (Bansal et al., 2020). On the other hand, metallic dendrites are formed during the battery cycle, causing a short circuit (Miao et al., 2019).

Lithium alloys (Li-M, where M = Sn and Si, for example) have a specific capacity greater than graphite, but a high volumetric variation occurs, causing cracks and capacity loss. For instance, lithium-silicon alloy (Li15Si4) has a specific capacity greater than metallic lithium (4200Ah/kg). However, changes in volume of up to 280% decrease the diffusion of lithium and high electrical resistance (Miao et al., 2019; Passerini and Scrosati, 2016).

A different type of anode is the conversion electrodes, formed by nanosized metal oxides (MO, where M = Co, Fe, Cu, Mn, and Ni, for example). The material has a different electrochemical process, in which the metal initially in the form of metallic oxide turns into metallic during the lithiation, and the lithium metallic turns into lithium oxide. It has a high specific capacity and stability, minimizing thermal risks, however, it has problems in the charge-discharge cycle (Miao et al., 2019; Passerini and Scrosati, 2016).

Changes in the battery electrolyte are being studied to make it safer, avoiding flammable solvents without compromising performance since polymeric electrolytes have a conductivity of 10−5S/cm (Kamaya et al., 2011). A type of electrolyte that has been evaluated is the aqueous electrolyte, but to increase the electrochemical voltage, it is necessary to use a very high salt concentration. As a result, it exceeds the number of water molecules and makes it difficult to commercialize (Miao et al., 2019; Suo et al., 2015).

An electrolyte that is being developed and is considered very promising is an ionic liquid; for instance, molten salts at temperatures below 100 °C or even at room temperature. They have almost zero vapor pressure, high-temperature stability, large electrochemical stability window, do not have flammable components, and in addition have good ionic conductivity. The biggest disadvantage of this material is the high cost, which can be bypassed with commercialization (Osada et al., 2016).

Solid-state electrolytes are considered to have the same conductivity as conventional organic liquid electrolytes at room temperature, as they have no flammability and their conductivity reaches around 10−2S/cm at 50–80 °C. Different solid-state electrolytes have been investigated to improve their ionic conductivity and their chemical and electrochemical stability. The solid electrolyte with the highest ionic conductivity is Li3N with 6 × 10−3S/cm at room temperature; on the other hand, its electrochemical decomposition potential is too low to be used in batteries (Kamaya et al., 2011).

Among the solid electrolytes currently explored, there are sulfides such as Li2SP2S5 (LPS), grenades as Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO), ceramic as LiSICONs (Lithium Super Ion Conductors) that use the grain boundary conductivity with an expected performance similar to that of liquid, glass-ceramic such as Li7P3S11 and glassy materials such as Li2S/SiS2/Li3PO (Crabtree, 2019; Kamaya et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2019). Kamaya et al. (2011) developed a lithium superionic conductor composed of Li10GeP2S12 with 12 mS/cm conductivity at room temperature non-explosive, having high electrochemical potential and not volatile (Kamaya et al., 2011).

Despite the evolution of the lithium-ion battery components, there is a great deal of research focusing on energy storage improvement. The lithium-air battery is a widely-mentioned battery model eyed by private companies such as Toyota Motor Corp, IBM, and BMW. The anode and the cathode are made of lithium and air, respectively. The reaction between the Li-ions and the oxygen present in the cathode releases energy, having a high energy density similar to gasoline. However, this battery has limited cathode stability and high lithium anode reactivity (Passerini and Scrosati, 2016; Rajashekara, 2013).

In order to prevent the risk of interruption of the lithium supply, sodium-ion batteries (NIBs) have been developed. The biggest problem is establishing the electrodes since the graphite anode cannot be used due to the very large sodium ion for the graphite layers, and only a few cathodes have been reported for such battery (Passerini and Scrosati, 2016). Several other types of batteries are also developed, such as the lithium-sulfur battery, magnesium batteries, aluminum-ion battery, and structural changes to LIBs, such as the new electrode design with a carbon nanotube-like structure mentioned by Cao et al. (2011) (Cao et al., 2011; Passerini and Scrosati, 2016).

Concerning the environmental impacts, according to Deng et al. (2017) and Lopez et al. (2021), lithium-sulfur batteries are more environmentally friendly than NMC batteries achieving up to 90% less impact (Deng et al., 2017; Lopez et al., 2021). Similar achievements have been observed in regard to Al-ion batteries, which have high carbon footprint in their production (Salgado Delgado et al., 2019). Manganese-based batteries are also considered environmentally friendly for storage systems (Fichtner, 2011). A comparative study between these batteries and LIB are necessary to conclude which battery has a lower environmental impact.

The use of cobalt, lithium, aluminum, nickel and manganese has a high carbon footprint due to the primary production, leading to the development of green technologies to decrease negative impacts on the environment. Biobatteries as an emerging technology have been studied due to the low environmental impacts of the life cycle when compared to chemical batteries, reducing the environmental load, in which sugar batteries may have higher energy density than LIBs (Adekunle et al., 2017; Bowie et al., 2020; Manzetti and Mariasiu, 2015).

5. LIBs as a source of critical metals

Some components of current LIBs are considered critical worldwide due to the strategic application and high supply risk (Duarte Castro et al., 2021; European Commission, 2017; Jowitt et al., 2018; Mansur et al., 2021). Since 2008, the European Union (EU) has updated a list of critical materials to them according to the market, technology, and product development. The current list (2020) has antimony, barite, beryllium, bismuth, borate, cobalt, coking coal, fluorspar, gallium, germanium, hafnium, helium, indium, lithium, magnesium, natural graphite, natural rubber, niobium, phosphate rock, phosphorus, scandium, silicon metal, tantalum, tungsten, vanadium, platinum group metals, rare earth elements, bauxite, lithium, titanium, and strontium (European Commision, 2020). The International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) conducts the recycling efficiency of batteries (ISO, 2015).

For the U.S. Department of Energy, the materials are classified according to fundamental criteria in the short and medium-term: the importance of metal for clean energy generation, supply risk, the availability of the natural mineral in the world, production, and scarcity perspective (U.S. Department of Energy, 2010). The critical materials, or key materials, presently on the list are aluminum (bauxite), antimony, arsenic, barite, beryllium, bismuth, cesium, chromium, cobalt, fluorspar, gallium, germanium, natural graphite, hafnium, helium, indium, lithium, magnesium, manganese, niobium, platinum group metals, potash, rare earth elements (REEs), rhenium, rubidium, scandium, strontium, tantalum, tellurium, tin, titanium, tungsten, uranium, vanadium, zirconium (USGS, 2018).

In Brazil, the expression “strategic metals” or "strategic materials" is used, preferably when it comes to raw materials heavily dependent on imports and minerals Brazil stands out for their abundance, natural reserves, and production. Moreover, also regarded as strategic are the ones currently sought-after and likely to boom in the coming years. The current list, to be updated until 2030, contains the following elements: REEs aluminum, chromium; cobalt; copper; gallium; gold; indium; iron; lead; lithium; manganese; molybdenum; nickel; niobium; palladium; phosphor; platinum; tantalum; tin; titanium; tungsten; vanadium; zinc; zirconium (MCTIC, 2018).

Based on that, it is worth pointing out that LIBs may be a future source of materials with scarcity of supply in the short-term. REEs contained in electric engines; cobalt, lithium, and graphite in batteries (vanadium in redox flow batteries); and tantalum and palladium in power electronics are examples of critical metals present in HEV and EV (Cunha et al., 2015; Iglesias-Émbil et al., 2020; Polyak, 2019; Uhrig et al., 2016). As the use of HEV and EV increases, the demand for such critical metals will rise, resulting in a different type of waste material with economic importance (Gu et al., 2017).

Besides, the importance of LIB recycling is also associated with the availability of materials in each country. For instance, the EU is heavily dependant on Russia (91%) and the Democratic Republic of Congo (7%) when it comes to cobalt supply. For lithium supply, Chile (78%), the USA (8%) and Russia (4%) are the main sourcing countries (Alves Dias et al., 2018; European Commision, 2020; European Commission, 2017). As countries in the EU plan to ban ICE vehicles, and projections estimate more than 125 million HEV and EV worldwide until 2030 (Crabtree, 2019; Lebedeva et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2019), the recycling of LIBs of these vehicles at the end of life could turn out to be a resource of critical elements within Europe. The recycled material could be used as raw material to produce new EV batteries, which meets the definitions of circular economy (Alessia et al., 2021; Kalmykova et al., 2018; Kirchherr et al., 2017). Nowadays, this sort of recycling is almost negligible, as in Australia, where only 2% of batteries are recycled (Tabelin et al., 2021).

As depicted in Fig. 7, the circular economy paradigm is getting more relevant every day, replacing the “end-of-life” concept with the combination of reducing, reuse, recycling activities in the production/distribution, and consumption processes of all stakeholders. The circular economy's main aim is to combine economic and environmental aspects without neglecting social issues for sustainable development, creating environmental quality, economic prosperity, and social equity for the beneﬁt of current and future generations (Aljerf and Choukaife, 2016; Kirchherr et al., 2017).

The popularity of the circular economy (CE) concept brings new LIB recycling routes into light, targeting the recovery of a broad spectrum of compounds, thus reducing the environmental impact associated with LIB production and consumption. The stages of the circular economy are highly interdependent. For instance, to accomplish the expected CO2 reduction from LIB-powered transportation, the energy for their production should ideally come from renewable sources. Therefore, a CE also depends on environmental, political, and ﬁnancial conditions, turning it into a living and complex organism (Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019).

In CE, remanufacturing the batteries can decrease the environmental impact in all relevant sustainability indicators, especially regarding resource consumption and reducing greenhouse warming potential (Cantzler et al., 2020; Díaz-Ramírez et al., 2020). In combination with reuse and recycling activities, it may improve sustainability and reduce production costs significantly(Kampker et al., 2016).

Furthermore, the promotion of renewable energies and the circular economy (including shared vehicles or the changes in designs that allow reuse and recycling) will maximize the benefits of the change for electric vehicles (Bobeth and Kastner, 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Rallo et al., 2020).

On the other hand, countries worldwide should change their energy matrix decreasing the energy-related CO2 emissions. For instance, according to the Sustainable Development Report 2020, the gap of the SDG 13 (Climate Action) is associated to the CO2 emission of China, the USA, and the European Union, which altogether amount to 50% of global emission. For instance, the main challenge to Sweden's CO2 emissions in regard to energy generation results from the fact that its energy supply relies on nuclear energy, oil, biofuels and hydraulic energy. On the other hand, developing countries have improved their actions against climate changes: only Bhutan, Costa Rica, Ethiopia, India, Kenya, and the Philippines have made efforts in the world to hold global warming below 2 °C. In the case of India, the achievements for SDG 13 have improved (Sachs et al., 2020).

Recycling processes are a fundamental aspect of the circular economy, as they enable the recovery of different materials and metals from urban waste as a secondary source, reducing the consumption of natural resources(Grigoropoulos et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2017).

6. Recycling routes and their challenges

Unlike other batteries, LIBs present lower environmental risks, longer life, compact design, better resistance to self-discharge, greater resistance to high temperatures, and greater voltage output compared with other types of batteries (Chen et al., 2020). These advantageous characteristics make them attractive for industrial or urban mobility applications (Passerini and Scrosati, 2016). Aiming for the circular economy system, recycling routes for other types of batteries are being adapted to support LIB. Processes are designed according to the components of LIBs, their structures, and charge-storage mechanisms. Further ahead, consolidated processes and leading-edge research to recover materials from EV and HEV batteries are presented.

6.1. Consolidated processes

The processes further described are patents from companies that already work on the recycling sector, not necessarily an existent route used by them. Such processes were originally designed for other types of batteries, e.g., NiMH, alkaline, and lead-acid, and then modified to support peculiar characteristics of LIBs and specific goals, such as materials and target metals and risks of explosions (Assefi et al., 2020; Pagliaro and Meneguzzo, 2019; Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020). Some processes focused on extracting a few products, whereas others aimed to recover virtually all battery components achieving the circular economy.

6.1.1. AkkuSer Oy

AkkuSer Oy is a Finnish company focused on recycling Li-ion, NiMH, alkaline, lead-acid, and Ni–Cd batteries (Akkuser, 2020; Pudas et al., 2015). The plant was installed in Nivala in 2006, with a recycling capacity of 1000–4000 ton/year of discarded batteries. The materials are screened through mechanical processing for further refining and treatment (Lebedeva et al., 2017; Pudas et al., 2015). Therefore, the process also called Dry-Technology is used in the production of metal concentrates for refinery industries (Akkuser, 2020; Pudas et al., 2015).

The process route is depicted in Figure S4 for LCO batteries. First, the batteries are classified, and the cases are removed. The LIBs are ground at 40–50 °C and 100–400 rpm, removing dust, hydrogen, and oxygen gases by cyclonic separation, avoiding fire risk. The gases are filtered so that light plastics and cardboard can be removed and then sent to the NMH batteries recycling process on the nickel smelting step as an energy source (Akkuser, 2020; Pudas et al., 2015).

Particle sizes between 1.3 and 2.5 cm from the first crushing are sent to the second crushing, at room temperature, at 1000–1200 rpm to decrease the particle size to less than 0.6 cm for further magnetic separation. The iron fraction will be recovered by smelting, and a powder composed of copper and cobalt is obtained (Pudas et al., 2015), which may be separated by aqueous processing (leaching + separation) (Botelho Junior et al., 2019b; Kumar et al., 2017; Tesfaye et al., 2017).

6.1.2. Retriev Technologies Incorporated

The American company Retriev Technologies Incorporated, formerly known as Toxco, founded in 1984, is currently the leader in the battery recycling industry (lead-acid, Li-ion and polymer types, Ni–Cd, alkaline, NiMH, and primary batteries) in the USA and Canada with a capacity of 4500 tons/year (Ferg et al., 2019; Lebedeva et al., 2017; Smith and Swoffer, 2013). As a company with many years of experience investing in research and innovation, Retriev has several patents. The LIB recycling closed-loop process is shown in Figure S5 depicting a route focusing on most battery constituents' recovery. However, the company is not fully operating currently, it only grinds and separates the parts, and the refining of metals is delegated to other companies (Retriev Technologies, 2020a; Smith and Swoffer, 2013).

The process starts with discarded LIBs sent for crushing in a hammer mill under an inert atmosphere and water spray to avoid the emission of particulates and the risk of any type of fire or explosion. Simultaneously, the inert atmosphere (N2 or noble gases) reduces the oxygen into low content, keeping the chances of bringing about an explosive environment during the milling process to almost zero (Abbasi and Abbasi, 2007).

After crushing, the material obtained is sieved, separating the plastic, Al, and Cu concentrate, keeping in the process only the carbon and the cathode active material (Retriev Technologies, 2020b; Smith and Swoffer, 2013).

The advantage of the Toxco route is the recovery of different parts of the battery. In the sieving step, granulometric separation may separate plastic from metallic fraction (Maisel et al., 2020), and then aluminum may be separated from copper by alkali leaching, for instance (Botelho Junior et al., 2021; Larouche et al., 2020). The remaining material is filtrated, dried, and heated at 400–700 °C, eliminating the binder and modifying the carbon surfaces, and sent to the flotation process for carbon recovery (85% purity), where it will be treated to be reused for LIB production. The heavier sludge separated is filtered, washed, dried, and then heated with the addition of LiOH at 400–850 °C to obtain a regenerated cathode material with specific stoichiometry for reuse in LIB production (Smith and Swoffer, 2013).

6.1.3. JX Nippon Mining & Metals corporation

The Japanese company of electronic materials, mining, and refining of non-ferrous metals and recycling designed the Tsuruga plant (Figure S6), responsible for recycling LIB with a capacity of 5000 tons/year (Ferg et al., 2019; JX Nippon Mining and Metals, 2020a). The process first focuses on separating active material from the cathode's current collector (aluminum), and secondly the Mn, Co, Ni, and Li recovery in different steps. As JX Nippon is interested in non-ferrous metals, its recycling process aims only for these metals, mostly found in the cathode (Yamaguchi and Hino, 2012; Yoshimi et al., 2013).

The first step consists of a grinding operation coupled to a vibrating sieve retaining particle larger than 100–200 mm composed of aluminum foils (current collector) (Yoshimi et al., 2013). The cathode-rich material with a particle size of 0.1–0.5 mm is sent to a leaching step in an acidic medium (H2SO4 3 mol/L), and the non-leach material graphite and organic materials are filtrated and incinerated for energy production (JX Nippon Mining and Metals, 2020b; Yamaguchi and Hino, 2012).

The selective separation of the metals is carried out by solvent extraction after pH correction (Yamaguchi and Hino, 2012). Such solvents were chosen due to their selectivity. As the pH of the solution changes, the organic solvent will remove a specific metallic ion from the aqueous media (Kislik, 2014; Schlesinger et al., 2011). For instance, in the pH range 0–1.5, the organic solvent D2EHPA is selective for ferric iron, whereas from pH 3.0 to 4.5, it separates nickel and cobalt together from aqueous solution to the organic phase. For this reason, in the process, cobalt is first separated at pH 4.2 using PC-88A, and nickel is separated from lithium-rich solution at pH 6.5 (Kislik, 2014). These recovered metals can be precipitated in carbonate form or electrolytically refined (Yamaguchi and Hino, 2012).

6.1.4. Umicore

Umicore is a global company located in at least 8 countries with extensive technology and material recycling portfolio. Umicore Cobalt & Specialty Materials focuses on recycling, refining, and processing cobalt and nickel materials. In Hoboken (Belgium), the company has a plant with LIB and NiMH recycling processing capacity of 7000 ton/year (Cheret and Santén, 2005; Umicore, 2020a, 2020b).

The pyrometallurgical process currently performed is presented in Figure S7 (Cheret and Santén, 2005), which occurs only in a single vertical axis furnace. The LIBs are fed at the top of the furnace with coke and slag formers. The phases inside the furnace can be divided into three different stages: preheating zone, where the temperature slowly rises with the heated air from the bottom up to 300 °C; pyrolysis of plastic, which occurs at 700 °C generating energy to heat the gas in the first zone; and smelting and reduction of the metals, injecting air or oxygen-rich air preheated. At this stage, nickel-cobalt-copper alloy is produced, and the slag is composed of lithium, aluminum, silicon, and calcium (Cheret and Santén, 2005).

The slag can be sent to the construction industry or to recover metals (Loai Aljerf, 2015). Leaching and ion exchange steps can separate the metals in the alloy stream. According to Elwert et (2016), after acid leaching, the metallic ions can be separated by solvent extraction, and then a new cathode is produced (Cheret and Santén, 2005; Elwert et al., 2016; Umicore, 2020b).

6.1.5. Recupyl process

Recupyl is a French company operating in Europe, Asia, and North America offering recycling services for alkaline batteries and LIBs with a capacity of 110 tons/year(Recupyl, 2020a; Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019). The process currently performed by the company involves mechanical separation and chemical treatment steps, as shown in Figure S8 (Recupyl, 2020b; Tedjar and Foudraz, 2006).

After the previous separation, the LIBs are ground in a rotary shear machine at 11 rpm releasing internal parts. A second crushing is performed in an impact mill at 90 rpm. Both crushing steps are performed under an inert atmosphere with CO2, argon, or a mixture of both, to avoid an explosion. Particles larger than 3 mm are sent to magnetic separation aiming for iron; and aluminum and copper are separated from plastics by the densimetric table. The fraction smaller than 3 mm is sent to a 500 μm sieve to separate the remaining copper (Tedjar and Foudraz, 2006).

Particles smaller than 500 μm are water-washed aiming for soluble lithium recovery in order to obtain carbonate salt (Porvali et al., 2019). The remaining material is leached by sulfuric acid in the presence of iron for both carbon (solid phase) and cobalt recovery, the latter being obtained after electrolysis. The remaining Lithium is obtained by phosphoric acid leaching, in which the cobalt that was also leached is recovered, adding sodium hypochlorite at pH between 2.3 and 2.8 (Tedjar and Foudraz, 2006; Velázquez-Martínez et al., 2019).

6.1.6. Duesenfeld GmbH

The German company Duesenfeld GmbH designed a plant located in Wendeburg to recycle LIBs in a closed-loop route with a capacity of 1500 tons/year (Duesenfeld, 2020; Ferg et al., 2019). The flowsheet currently carried out is shown in Figure S9 (Hanisch, 2019; Hanisch et al., 2019). The recycling process starts with a discharging step to avoid explosions (Ojanen et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2020), a manual disassembly, out of which large battery systems are removed, such as electronic controls. The batteries are ground under inert atmosphere (N2 or CO2) (Hanisch et al., 2019).

After crushing, the drying step below 80 °C aims for the evaporation of electrolytes avoiding the formation of organic fluorine compounds that will be condensed for reuse on LIB production (Kosaraju, 2012). The following step involves a second crushing and separation of copper, iron, aluminum, and plastic. The remaining material is treated by a hydrometallurgical route: leaching and solvent extraction (Porvali et al., 2019). Carbon is recovered by filtration after sulfuric acid leaching, and metallic ions are separated in different streams by Cyanex 301, Cyanex 272, and D2EHPA. Lithium precipitate is obtained as phosphate or carbonate (Hanisch, 2019; Hanisch et al., 2019).

Compared with the Tsuruga process (6.1.3), the German route uses Fe/NaOH after carbon recovery for copper and aluminum precipitation, remaining from the separation step previous to leaching. In the solvent extraction step, Cyanex 272 and 301 are used for cobalt and nickel extraction, in which these organic extractants are long-established (Crundwell et al., 2011). After reextraction, cobalt, nickel, and manganese sulfate can be used with lithium phosphate or carbonate as raw material for NMC cathode production. The route goes into a closed-loop towards zero-waste processing in accordance with the circular economy definition (Atia et al., 2019; Kalmykova et al., 2018; Kirchherr et al., 2017; Korhonen et al., 2018; Mossali et al., 2020a; Pagliaro and Meneguzzo, 2019; Paletta et al., 2019).

6.2. New trends in battery recycling

Despite the current process and technology already developed, studies evaluating new approaches for LIB recycling have been carried out. The objectives vary: safety on dismantling step, electricity recovery before recycling, pre-treatment improvement, mechanical separation, and processing routes. Several process improvements and the development of new routes are being explored to solve or minimize issues. Three main routes have been explored to recover metals from LIBs: pyro-, hydro-, and biohydrometallurgy (Zheng et al., 2018).

The routes studied as well as the aforementioned processes start with the battery dismantling step, either manually (as Duesenfeld GmbH) or using industrial equipment (as Retriev and Recupyl), with or without discharging step (as Duesenfeld GmbH), when an exothermic reaction may occur between Li and oxygen in the atmosphere which would cause explosions (Sonoc et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, in the electrode, water reacts with fluorinated salts forming hydrofluoric acid - an undesirable product due to its high corrosive power and toxicity. Under high temperatures (as the Umicore process), reactions can occur inside the batteries producing gases generating battery combustion, forming toxic compounds such as dioxins and halogenated organic compounds (Hanisch et al., 2019; Xu, 2014). Organic solvents as electrolytes ignite at 120 °C producing flammable gases such as methane (Wuschke et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2018), and PVDF binders may also form toxic gases (Larsson et al., 2014). A few examples are pointed out to assess the current innovations in LIBs recycling, as follows:

6.2.1. Pretreatment

The pretreatment of LIBs involves the discharge, grinding, and separation of the main constituents before the chemical processing (thermal or aqueous) (Kim et al., 2021). This step is very important since serious environmental issues and safety problems may be caused if the steps are not well designed and controlled, however, it can lead to metal losses (Huang et al., 2019; Mayyas et al., 2019).

Thermal degradation may also occur if the following is not avoided: LCO cathode decomposes above 150 °C, NMC at 210 °C, LMO at 260 °C, and LFP at 310 °C, releasing O2 (Lu et al., 2013). The electrolyte solution also degrades, releasing flammable gases such as H2, CH4, and C2H4 (Lisbona and Snee, 2011). Above 90 °C, the solid-electrolyte interface decomposes, neglecting the anode, which reacts with electrolyte forming flammable gases(Winslow et al., 2018). The electrolyte decomposes above 200 °C and can form CO2, C2H4, halogenated organic compounds, and hydrogen fluoride, the latter also generated when PVDF is degraded. For this reason, some EV and HEV batteries are composed of polymeric electrolytes avoiding harmful gases release (Hanisch, 2019; Lisbona and Snee, 2011).

Furthermore, discarded LIBs have residual energy stored, as an electronic circuit does not allow the battery to discharge below 3V, avoiding performance problems (Sonoc et al., 2015). Thermal or mechanical pretreatment can cause a short circuit in the batteries causing a fast release of such stored energy and a rapid increase in temperature, causing explosions (Kim et al., 2021). Therefore, it is necessary to structure a process that avoids the above-mentioned risks, as the battery discharge procedure (Huang et al., 2018).

Battery discharge can be carried out by promoting a controlled short circuit or using a resistor, storing residual energy (Mossali et al., 2020a; Widijatmoko et al., 2020). To ensure the safety of the process, the temperature must be kept below 90 °C, avoiding the risks associated with high temperatures. Moreover, when the batteries reach 0V, the Li-ion is immobilized, forming a thermodynamically stable cathode, avoiding the safety risks associated with lithium's reaction with oxygen or water (Sonoc et al., 2015).

A method widely spread in the literature for discharging LIBs is submerging them in saline solutions since it is a fast, easy, and low-cost method. Ojanen et al. (2018) studied the discharging process in saline and their products in different conditions: 5%, 10%, and 20% using NaCl, NaSO4, FeSO4, and ZnSO4. Results have shown that NaCl solution was the best option compared with sulfate salts because sulfate precipitates were deposited on the silver threads avoiding the short circuit and the discharging (Ojanen et al., 2018). However, the process generated chlorine gas and undesired precipitates – losses of Al, Co, Li, Cu, Mn, and volatile organic compounds, mainly dimethyl carbonate, were detected (Li et al., 2016a).

Graphite and Cu powder may also be used, but the instability for large-scale application makes the physical method unfeasible. Yao et al. (2020) demonstrated that sodium chloride and iron sulfate are the best discharge solutions despite the gas release, metal losses, and organic molecules formed from broken organic solvents and binders (Yao et al., 2020).

Wuschke et al. (2019) stated that the grinding of the LIBs must occur after full discharge, avoiding the risk of fire and explosions(Wuschke et al., 2019). However, despite the ways of discharging the batteries mentioned above, the voltage measured right after this process does not correctly correspond to the energy stored in the batteries (Rouhi et al., 2021). Hence, the charge still stored must be considered before the comminution step and appropriate precautions must be taken. The thermal control method can be observed in the AkkuSer Oy process, maintaining the crushing temperature-controlled to 40–50 °C, while Umicore process gradually heats the batteries evaporating the electrolyte before exothermic reactions occur for further thermal treatment (Cheret and Santén, 2005; Pudas et al., 2015). The liquid nitrogen may also be used for cryogenic cooling down to −196 °C, turning the Li inside the battery unreactive before shredding (Sonoc et al., 2015).

As in the Retriev process, Tedjar and Foudraz (2006) mentioned a crushing process with water, but hydrogen gas and hydrogen fluoride were formed (Smith and Swoffer, 2013; Tedjar and Foudraz, 2006). Mayyas et al. (2019) suggested the procedure under stirring to prevent hydrogen gas accumulation, further maintaining an oxygen-poor atmosphere reducing the risk of explosions (Mayyas et al., 2019). According to Takahashi et al. (2020), ultrasound can decrease the distribution of particle size (Takahashi et al., 2020).

The most usual method to prevent risks during crushing, with or without the battery discharge, is maintaining the inert atmosphere: N2, CO2, Ar, or a mixture of gases is used during the grinding, transforming an oxygen-poor atmosphere (Harper et al., 2019; Ojanen et al., 2018). This method is shown in Duesenfeld GmbH, Recupyl, and Retriev processes.

6.2.2. Separation

The separation of LIBs components aims to concentrate materials with similar properties for an improvement in the recovery rate (Huang et al., 2018). Manual disassembly (as in the Duesenfeld GmbH process) is commonly reported, but it is a time-consuming process and requiring manual labor and additional cost. Therefore, it is not viable for industrial-scale (He et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; W. Zhang et al., 2018a).

As previously described, different equipment and approaches are applied to industrial viability. The separation after crushing the LIBs in streams makes the recovery of battery components easier. Magnetic and granulometric separation is widely used (Retriev, JX, Recupyl, and Duesenfeld processes), as is the case with iron and aluminum/copper foils.

In the positive electrode, aluminum foils are bound to the cathode. To separate them and to obtain a cathode-rich material, He et al. (2015) used organic solvent N–N-dimethylformamide to dissolve PVDF binder (He et al., 2015), and Chen and Zhou (2014) tested N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone in an ultrasound bath (Chen and Zhou, 2014). As a result, the recovered aluminum foils may be used for new battery production or to supply the aluminum industry, and the cathode may be regenerated for reuse or to produce a variety of compounds based on the metal components of the oxide.

According to Wang et al. (2016), LiCoO2 was ground with various additives, and it was found that ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) was the most suitable grinding reagent, which enabled the recovery of almost 98% of Co and 99% of Li. The mechano-chemical method transforms the crystal structure of LiCoO2 into a disordered system, allowing the extraction of Co and Li easily by acid leaching at room temperature (Larouche et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2016).

Pagnanelli et al. (2017) studied the influence of grinding equipment on leaching performance, stating that a treatment in a double-axis grinder followed by a hammer mill is an efficient pretreatment for metal recovery (Pagnanelli et al., 2017). Similar achievements were found by other authors (Asadi Dalini et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2017; Takahashi et al., 2020; Wuschke et al., 2019). Particle size above 1 mm is mainly composed of plastic, steel, aluminum, and copper, whereas particles with less than 1 mm contain Co, Mn, Li, Ni. Metallic and non-metallic phases can then be separated by density and ferrous and non-ferrous phases by magnetic separation (Pagnanelli et al., 2016). Component classification can also occur by flotation separating the active material from the cathode and anode (as in Retriev process) (G. Zhang et al., 2018).

The thermal method is used to remove electrolyte, carbon impurities and binders (Li et al., 2017). Zhang et al. (2018) showed that it is possible to remove organic binders in a pyrolysis process under a nitrogen atmosphere at 500 °C, and the remaining pyrolysis products can be removed by ultrasound bath (G. Zhang et al., 2018). Nonetheless, thermal treatment releases toxic gases, in turn requiring treatment.

Industry 4.0 is also discussed for LIB recycling for process control and screening of battery types. It is necessary that the robotic system be flexible and intelligent, so it can differentiate and separate batteries of different types and formats and also be cheap, making recycling a more attractive process (Harper et al., 2019).

6.2.3. Pyrometallurgical route

Pyrometallurgy is a thermal process in elevated temperatures with fast kinetics that consists of separating the slag from the materials of interest, which are concentrated in another phase. The processing depends on temperature, time, purge gases, and flux addition (Makuza et al., 2021). For the recycling of LIBs, pyrometallurgy is used to help the hydrometallurgical process. Li et al. (2016a, 2016b) explored the feasibility of the reaction between the active material of the cathode and anode, LiCoO2, and graphite, in an inert atmosphere heating up to 1000 °C. After wet magnetic separation, three products were obtained: water-soluble lithium carbonate phase, cobalt ferromagnetic, and residual carbon as a water-insoluble phase (Li et al., 2016b).

Lombardo et al. (2019) studied different pyrolysis times and temperatures to reduce the NMC cathode using the graphite anode, where lithium carbonate, an oxide mixture, and carbon were obtained at 700 °C under reductive atmosphere (Lombardo et al., 2019). The oxidative atmosphere may also be an option for LIB pyrolysis, but fluoride by-products must be treated (Lombardo et al., 2020). Peng et al. (2019) studied the nitration-roasting-leaching process for Li recovery. First, nitric acid was a mixture with the LIBs at 70 °C for 5h, roasting at 250 °C and followed by water leaching, which removed Li selectively for high-pure Li2CO3 product (Peng et al., 2019).

Hu et al. (2021a, 2021b) studied the recycling of Li-ion batteries by thermal processing, in which Li, such as halides, was recovered in the flue dust, and Co was obtained in metallic form. In the case of NMC batteries, a Co–Ni–Mn alloy is obtained in the slag, and Li was recovered in the flue dust as carbonate or fluoride. In both cases, efficiency stood at 100% on the lab scale (Hu et al., 2021a). On the industrial scale using Electric Arc Furnace in two trials, (the) efficiency achieved up to 98%. Li was obtained as carbonate from the flue dust whereas the slag was composed of Co–Ni–Mn alloy. Since lime is used for slag formation, a CaO–Al2O3 slag can be generated as a byproduct of the recycling process adding economical benefit (Hu et al., 2021b).

6.2.4. Hydrometallurgical route

The main advance of hydrometallurgical processing includes the treatment of complex composition, the recovery of metals in low concentration and obtaining highly pure products (Asadi Dalini et al., 2020; Atia et al., 2019; Larouche et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020). The most inorganic acids used for LIBs leaching are sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and nitric acid (Assefi et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2016).

Furthermore, many works have now been carried out with organic acid, as they are easy to degrade, in addition to producing less toxic gases during leaching (Golmohammadzadeh et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2018). Citric acid and DL-malic acid have shown promising results for battery recycling (Golmohammadzadeh et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018). Chabhadiya et al. (2021) depicted a two-step leaching of NMC cathode battery towards environmentally sustainable route and less negative impacts, in which lithium and copper were first extracted selectively by oxalic acid. The residue composed of cobalt, nickel and manganese oxalates was then leached by sulfuric acid (Chabhadiya et al., 2021).

For cobalt leaching, a reducing agent may be required, and hydrogen peroxide is widely used for that matter (Li et al., 2017; Pagnanelli et al., 2017). Ferrous iron can also be used as a reducing agent, as demonstrated by Diaz et al. (2020) on electrochemical-assisted leaching, where a current is used to regenerate ferrous iron by replacing the use of hydrogen peroxide (Diaz et al., 2020). Ultrasound-assisted leaching also demonstrated an improvement in metals extraction in acid medium due to the impact of bubbles breaking in the cavitation process caused by ultrasonic waves (Li et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2020). Besides, after this process, the graphite is separated from the materials and can be recycled for graphene production (He et al., 2021).

After leaching, a selective separation is required to obtain high purity products, and ion exchange techniques are widely used, as in the case of solvent extraction. Pagnanelli et al. (2016) used D2EHPA for impurities removal (Mn) and Cyanex 272 to separate cobalt from nickel (Pagnanelli et al., 2016). According to Hu et al. (2017), cobalt and nickel may be separated from a similar solution by PC88A at different pH values (Hu et al., 2017). In both cases, manganese, cobalt, nickel, and lithium, which are highly pure products, can be obtained for further applications.

Chelating resins may also be used for solid-liquid separation (Badawy et al., 2014; Botelho Junior et al., 2019b; Kołodyńska et al., 2020). The technique uses ion exchangers that have an order of selectivity, that is, it has a preference for some elements than others. In the case of chelating resin Lewatit TP 220, with a bis-picolylamine functional group, it is more selective for cobalt and nickel than manganese and aluminum, making the separation of these elements possible (Botelho Junior et al., 2019a). Even though solvent extraction is more explored than chelating resins, the use of resins is advantageous as it eases the operation and also due to its low cost (Gupta and Mukherjee, 1990; Inamuddin, 2012).

Advances on solid-liquid extraction have recently explored the ionic liquids for the dissolution of Li, Co, Ni, and Mn oxides or solvent extraction for a selective separation in order to obtain high product (Garole et al., 2020; Larouche et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2018). By the same token, Cyphos IL-101 has shown to be promising for metallic ions separation (Xu et al., 2020).

The precipitation process may also be carried out. Li can be obtained by adding sodium phosphate or carbonate (He et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2016; Meshram et al., 2015). Co, Mn, and Ni can be obtained by adding oxalic acid or increasing the pH for hydroxide or carbonate product (Meshram et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2013). Besides, Mn can also be obtained through potassium permanganate, Ni through dimethylglyoxime, and Co through ammonium oxalate (Chen and Zhou, 2014; Huang et al., 2016).

In the case of LCO batteries, in which cathodes are previously disassembled using 1 mol/L of H2SO4 under ultrasound agitation, the leach solution was composed of Co, Li, Na, and sulfate anions. The cobalt obtaining as hydroxide was carried out by precipitation increasing the pH to 11 (Jo and Myung, 2019). On the other hand, in the case of a multielementary solutions, as the hydrometallurgical processing of NMC batteries, the use of precipitation by carbonate or hydroxide couldn't selectively separate nickel and cobalt, for instance (Jackson, 1986).

If iron is present in the solution, as it may be released from cylindrical cells of the case material, the precipitation for iron removal causes co-precipitation of different metallic ions such as cobalt and nickel (de Fátima da Silva et al., 2020). In a different case, copper can be separated from the leaching solution of NMC cylindrical cell batteries as sulfide (Perez et al., 2020).

6.2.5. Biohydrometallurgical route

It consists of a hydrometallurgical process, in which fungi or bacteria carry out the leaching. Literature reports using such a technique for metals extraction from electronic devices and mining ores or waste. Starting with the microorganism culture process, each microorganism has its own best conditions for the process, for instance: the pH, temperature, the composition of the culture medium for cell growth, time, and solid-liquid ratio (Arda et al., 2019; Brisson et al., 2016; Reed et al., 2016; Utimura et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2018).

Each microorganism will present different results. The fungus Aspergillus niger produces citric, oxalic, gluconic, and malic acids on LIB recycling, in which all Cu and Li were leached and 77% of Mn, 75% of Al, 64% of Co, and 54% of Ni (Bahaloo-Horeh and Mousavi, 2017; Horeh et al., 2016). Sedlakova-Kadukova et al. (2017) explored the bacteria Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans and Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans that produce sulfuric acid during bioleaching, in which cobalt is reduced from +3 to +2 without the use of a reducing agent (Sedlakova-Kadukova et al., 2017).

The process has a very high potential for industrial applications, being eco-friendly as a bonus. The hydrometallurgical route's main drawbacks might be the low kinetic rate since the biohydrometallurgical process takes days to achieve the same efficiency as the acid leaching (Awasthi and Li, 2017). Further separation techniques after bioleaching are pretty much the same as the hydrometallurgical route.

6.2.6. Electrometallurgy

Electrometallurgy is a process for refining (electrorefining) and production (electrowinning, electroplating, and electroforming) from a solution containing metals throughout electrolysis. It is commonly used at the end of the process for metallic products with high purity. Bae et al. (2016) designed a system in which Li was recovered from the cathode by a permeable membrane, and then further electrodeposited in order to obtain metallic lithium (Bae et al., 2016).

Rafsanjani-Abbasi et al. (2018) evaluated the ascorbic-assisted sulfuric leaching of LIBs to use the ascorbic acid as both a reducing and a leaching agent; such combined system is used as a morphological modifier during electrodeposition of LiCo(CO)4 compound, to avoid corrosion of carbon steel (Rafsanjani-Abbasi et al., 2018). Falqueto et al. (2018) obtained cobalt by electrodeposition from LIB recycling, in which it was used for azo dye degradation combined with H2O2, which, in turn, converted Co into Co3O4, precisely the opposite of what occurs during acid leaching (Falqueto et al., 2018).

7. Future perspectives

LIBs for EV and HEV may abide by the same legislation as current lead-acid batteries do. At the end of their useful life, the batteries will be collected by the manufacturers, and new ones will be installed, avoiding risks of inappropriate disposal or accidents. As a result, LIBs collection and recycling rates will be higher than other waste resulting from electrical & electronic equipment (WEEE) (Armand et al., 2020; Espinosa and Mansur, 2019; Kumar et al., 2017; Mossali et al., 2020b; Yu et al., 2020).

The current processes for LIBs recycling presented here focus on the main parts: cathode, anode, cases, and current collectors (Al and Cu foils), due to their high content. The electrolyte is commonly removed and rarely recovered (Li et al., 2016a) since they are a mixture of different volatile organic compounds, and once the battery is ground, these organic compounds evaporate.

Some batteries present Nb in the cathode or anode composition, but it is hardly explored, making the current market share small compared with lithium-metals oxides and graphite; despite that, the potential of the technology makes these batteries part of the next generation (Babu and Shaijumon, 2020; Griffith et al., 2019).

As aforementioned, the most critical materials present in the EV and HEV batteries are graphite, Co, and Li, whereas Mn and Ni are considered critical and strategic for the USA and Brazil. The recovery of REE used in EV and HEV motors is poorly explored. China is the main producer of natural graphite (~64%) (Olson, 2020) and REEs (~63%) worldwide (Gambog, 2020). The Democratic Republic of Congo accounts for 72% of Co global production and 51% of global reserves (Shedd, 2020), and 55% of Li production worldwide is from Australia, and 51% of the reserves are in Chile (Jaskula, 2020). Li and Co content in batteries are around 2-7 wt% and 5-15 wt% (Garole et al., 2020), respectively, while in natural ores they stand at 0.01–1.9 wt% and 0.05–1.1 wt%, respectively (Crundwell et al., 2011; Mohr et al., 2012). It makes the LIBs a man-made ore.

It is worth mentioning that the growing demand for metals for LIBs production also has social effects, even enhancing the extraction and recycling rates. Co extraction in the Democratic Republic of Congo has caused severe problems for workers and residents through pollution, water, and food contamination (Cheyns et al., 2014; Pourret et al., 2015; Squadrone et al., 2016).

Aiming for the decarbonization for climate change mitigation, the demand of Li, Co, and graphite shall increase by around 965%, 585%, and 383%, respectively by 2050, being the top 3 mineral needs, followed by indium (241%), for photovoltaic panels, and vanadium (173%), for flow batteries (Sovacool et al., 2020). It will result in an increasing pressure for extraction in natural reserves.

The EV/HEV market increased from 165,000 vehicles to 9 million between 2004 and 2012, and it is expected to keep on rising in the following years. The micro-hybrid market tends to follow the increase, but it costs 10 times less than EV and HEV systems and amount to up to 50% of the car sales (10 times higher than HEV). By 2025, the LIB market shall have achieved around 30 billion dollars (Pillot, 2013).

There is a sustainable conundrum about EV and HEV addressing climate change/ecological conservation, social impact, and economic importance. The direct impact of the new generation of vehicles is not certain. Since some countries' energy matrix is considered non-renewable – coal, nuclear, and oil – the pollution generated by EVs can be transferred from urban centers to regions where electricity is generated. The scenario can be worse considering the increase in extractive activities.

The transition to a clean energy matrix will be intensively minerallike, resulting in negative impacts on the environment since the activity is not sustainable (Sovacool et al., 2020), and recycling can decrease such impacts and dependence on natural resources (Harper et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2017; Larcher and Tarascon, 2015). For instance, the Co extraction from LIBs could make the European Union less dependent on Russia and Congo (European Commission, 2017).

The concern about the LIB market's raw material supply makes international agencies, such as the World Economic Forum and Eurasian Resources Group, launch strategies for responsible sourcing focusing on the battery market, mainly for Co, to support global strategies (Sovacool et al., 2020).

LIB recycling will certainly decrease the negative impact on mining activities, but the growing demand for EV and HEV makes the primary resource still necessary. The search for new natural ores is receiving more attention to supply the current and near-future demand, as the commercial reserves are dwindling. It is clear that recycling is an important tool for sustainable development towards a circular economy, but human beings will still depend on primary sources for a while.

8. Conclusion

LIBs consumption for electric and hybrid vehicle consumption, focused on Europe, the USA, and BRICS countries shall increase worldwide; the main reason being the sustainable agreements to reduce the CO2 releases. It increases battery waste generation rich in critical metals, mainly Li and Co. Thus, recycling is necessary to achieve sustainable goals towards a circular economy. Among the recycling routes, the current process and future approaches have been analyzed. Hydro- and biohydrometallurgy can focus on future processes to be developed since less energy and less harmful chemical reagents are required (in the case of organic acids). Moreover, both routes allow the extraction of elements in low concentrations and obtain high-purity products. Besides, new processing will be developed following the advance in battery technology. Futures studies should evaluate the future market of EV/HEV worldwide to assess the economic feasibility for recycling in different scenarios and countries.
